events.fact: Commodore George Dewey's American squadron destroyed the Spanish Pacific fleet at the Battle of Manila Bay without the loss of a single American sailor.
President Herbert Hoover pressed a button from the White House to light the newly completed Empire State Building in New York, then the tallest building in the world.

block: On May 1, 1898, Commodore George Dewey led his squadron into Manila Bay and, with the order to fire when ready, destroyed the entire Spanish Pacific fleet in a single morning without losing one American sailor. On the same day in 1931, President Herbert Hoover pressed a button in Washington that lit the newly raised Empire State Building, a tower flung up in eighteen months at the depth of the Great Depression. A Steadfast citizen presses forward in his appointed task whether the field is a battle line or a half-built tower, trusting that the God who steadies the resolute crowns patient labor in His time.

events.fact: Confederate General Thomas 'Stonewall' Jackson was mortally wounded by his own men at Chancellorsville after his celebrated flank march; he died of pneumonia eight days later.
Good Housekeeping magazine was first published in Holyoke, Massachusetts, dedicated to the order and care of the American household.

block: On the night of May 2, 1863, after a brilliant flanking march at Chancellorsville, General Thomas 'Stonewall' Jackson was shot down by the volleys of his own North Carolina troops in the darkness and would die of his wounds eight days later. On the same day in 1885, Good Housekeeping went on sale in Holyoke, Massachusetts, a magazine devoted to the steady ordering and care of the home. Jackson, a devout man who served his cause unto death, and the quiet keepers of the household alike show that a Loyal citizen gives his whole strength to the post entrusted to him, mindful that He who searches the heart rewards faithfulness in the great charge and the small.

events.fact: Rhode Island became the first of the thirteen colonies to renounce its allegiance to King George III, repealing the oath to the Crown two months before the Declaration of Independence.
Dutch director Peter Minuit arrived at the island of Manhattan, where he soon secured it for the Dutch West India Company and established New Amsterdam.

block: On May 4, 1776, the Rhode Island General Assembly became the first colony to renounce its allegiance to King George III, striking the oath to the Crown from its law a full two months before the Continental Congress declared independence. On the same day in 1626, Peter Minuit landed at Manhattan to plant the Dutch settlement of New Amsterdam at the mouth of a great river. A Trustworthy citizen keeps his word and breaks faith only when a higher loyalty compels him, building lawfully and openly as those who must one day give account to God for every stewardship.

events.fact: Dr. John Gorrie of Florida received a United States patent for an ice-making machine, a pioneering step toward mechanical refrigeration and air conditioning.
The German airship Hindenburg burst into flames while mooring at Naval Air Station Lakehurst, New Jersey, killing thirty-six people and ending the age of the passenger airship.

block: On May 6, 1851, Dr. John Gorrie of Florida won a patent for a machine to make ice, an honest invention born of his desire to cool the rooms of fevered patients, and a forerunner of all refrigeration. On the same day in 1937, the great airship Hindenburg burst into flame as it moored at Lakehurst, New Jersey, and thirty-six souls perished in moments as a watching world looked on. The contrast of patient invention and sudden ruin reminds a Responsible citizen to labor diligently for the good of his neighbor while holding every proud work loosely, for our days and our achievements rest wholly in the hand of God.

events.fact: General Alfred Jodl signed Germany's unconditional surrender to the Allies at General Eisenhower's headquarters in Reims, France, ending the Second World War in Europe.
A German submarine torpedoed the liner Lusitania off the coast of Ireland, drowning nearly 1,200 people including 128 Americans and turning American sentiment toward war.

block: On May 7, 1945, in a schoolhouse at Reims, General Alfred Jodl signed Germany's unconditional surrender before General Eisenhower's command, and the long agony of war in Europe was at last fulfilled. Three decades earlier, on the same day in 1915, a German torpedo sent the liner Lusitania to the bottom off Ireland in eighteen minutes, taking nearly twelve hundred lives and stirring a reluctant America toward the fight. From the loss of the innocent to the hard-won peace, a Steadfast citizen learns to hold his ground through the long night of conflict, trusting that the God of hosts brings even the bloodiest struggle to its appointed end.

events.fact: General Zachary Taylor's outnumbered army won the Battle of Palo Alto near the Rio Grande, the first major engagement of the Mexican-American War.
President Harry Truman proclaimed Victory in Europe Day as the Allied nations celebrated the surrender of Nazi Germany.

block: On May 8, 1846, General Zachary Taylor's outnumbered force stood firm on the prairie at Palo Alto and turned back a larger Mexican army by the speed of its mobile artillery, opening the Mexican-American War. On the same day in 1945, President Harry Truman proclaimed Victory in Europe, yet soberly warned a rejoicing nation that the victory was only half won while war still raged in the Pacific. A free people endures the long campaign by pressing on after each hard-bought field, and an Enduring citizen presses likewise toward the finish, knowing that He who sustains the weary gives strength to those who wait upon Him.

events.fact: Benjamin Franklin published the 'Join, or Die' woodcut in the Pennsylvania Gazette, the first political cartoon in an American newspaper, urging the colonies to unite.
President Woodrow Wilson issued the proclamation establishing the first national Mother's Day, to be observed on the second Sunday of May.

block: On May 9, 1754, Benjamin Franklin printed his severed-snake woodcut 'Join, or Die' in the Pennsylvania Gazette, the first American political cartoon, calling the scattered colonies to bind themselves together for the common defense. On the same day in 1914, President Woodrow Wilson proclaimed the first national Mother's Day, setting aside a day for the public reverence and love owed to the mothers of the country. An Obedient citizen submits gladly to the lawful bonds that knit a people together and honors his father and mother as the commandment requires, taking up his place under the authority God has ordained.

events.fact: Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys, with Benedict Arnold, captured Fort Ticonderoga from the British, the first American offensive victory of the Revolution; Allen demanded surrender 'in the name of the Great Jehovah and the Continental Congress.'
The Golden Spike was driven at Promontory Summit, Utah, joining the Central Pacific and Union Pacific lines to complete the first transcontinental railroad.

block: On May 10, 1775, Ethan Allen and his Green Mountain Boys surprised the sleeping British garrison at Fort Ticonderoga and seized it for the Revolution, Allen demanding surrender 'in the name of the Great Jehovah and the Continental Congress.' On the same day in 1869, the Golden Spike was driven at Promontory Summit, Utah, joining East and West by rail and shrinking a journey of months into a single week. Whether storming a fort under God's name or hammering the last spike of a continental road, an Obedient citizen takes up the work set before him under rightful authority, confident that he labors first under the eye of the Great Jehovah.

events.fact: Peter Stuyvesant arrived at New Amsterdam to serve as director-general of New Netherland, where he would govern the Dutch colony for seventeen years.
Minnesota was admitted to the Union as the thirty-second state.

block: On May 11, 1647, Peter Stuyvesant stepped ashore at New Amsterdam to take up the hard task of governing a struggling Dutch colony, restoring order to a settlement nearly emptied by mismanagement. On the same day in 1858, Minnesota entered the Union as the thirty-second state, drawing another vast commonwealth under the ordered government of the Republic. An Obedient citizen takes his appointed place within the lawful frame of authority, whether founding a town in the wilderness or knitting a new state into the nation, submitting himself to the order God establishes among men.

events.fact: General Benjamin Lincoln surrendered Charleston, South Carolina, and over three thousand troops to the British, the worst American defeat of the Revolutionary War.
The Soviet Union lifted its eleven-month blockade of West Berlin, defeated by the massive American and British airlift that had supplied two million people by air.

block: On May 12, 1780, after a long siege, General Benjamin Lincoln was forced to surrender Charleston and more than three thousand men to the British, the heaviest American defeat of the entire Revolution. On the same day in 1949, the Soviet Union admitted defeat and lifted its eleven-month blockade of West Berlin, broken at last by an Anglo-American airlift that had fed two million people from the sky. The bitter surrender and the patient triumph both teach the Steadfast citizen to hold fast through reversal and siege alike, for the God who permits the dark day also rewards those who do not let go their resolve.

events.fact: English colonists led by Captain Christopher Newport went ashore to found Jamestown in Virginia, the first permanent English settlement in North America.
The United States Congress declared war on Mexico at the request of President James K. Polk, beginning the Mexican-American War.

block: On May 13, 1607, three small English ships landed some hundred colonists along the James River in Virginia, where they founded Jamestown and gave England its first lasting foothold in the New World. On the same day in 1846, Congress voted overwhelmingly to declare war on Mexico, committing the nation to a conflict that would reshape the map of the continent. From the planting of a fragile colony to the resolve of a young republic at war, a Steadfast citizen sets his hand to enduring works and does not turn back, knowing that the God who plants nations sustains those who persevere.

events.fact: The Lewis and Clark Corps of Discovery set out from Camp Dubois near St. Louis to explore the vast Louisiana Purchase and seek a route to the Pacific.
President Harry Truman recognized the new State of Israel only eleven minutes after its founding, making the United States the first nation to do so.

block: On May 14, 1804, the Corps of Discovery under Meriwether Lewis and William Clark pushed their keelboat into the Missouri River from Camp Dubois, embarking on the great expedition to map the lands beyond the frontier. On the same day in 1948, President Harry Truman, defying the counsel of his own State Department, recognized the State of Israel within eleven minutes of its birth, the first head of state in the world to do so. Both the explorer who ventures into the unknown and the leader who acts on conviction display the resolve of a Steadfast citizen, who holds his course against doubt and difficulty in dependence upon God.

events.fact: Congress passed the Act of May 16, 1866, authorizing the first copper-nickel five-cent piece, the coin still known as the nickel.
The United States Senate fell one vote short of convicting President Andrew Johnson on the eleventh article of impeachment, preserving the office of the presidency from removal over policy.

block: On May 16, 1866, Congress authorized a new five-cent piece of copper and nickel, the sturdy coin Americans still carry, struck to steady a currency unsettled by the Civil War. On the same day in 1868, the Senate came within a single vote of removing President Andrew Johnson, falling short on the eleventh article so that the presidency would not be cast down over a quarrel of policy rather than true crime. An Obedient citizen honors both the honest coin of daily commerce and the lawful restraints of the Constitution, submitting to the ordered government that God has given a free people to keep them from the rule of mere faction.

events.fact: Twenty-four merchants signed the Buttonwood Agreement beneath a tree on Wall Street, the founding compact of what became the New York Stock Exchange.
The first Kentucky Derby was run at Churchill Downs in Louisville, where the colt Aristides won before a crowd of ten thousand.

block: On May 17, 1792, twenty-four brokers gathered beneath a buttonwood tree on Wall Street and signed a short agreement to trade only with one another at fixed terms, laying the cornerstone of the New York Stock Exchange and seeking to restore trust after a financial panic. On the same day in 1875, the first Kentucky Derby was run at Churchill Downs, beginning an American tradition that endures to this day. A Steadfast citizen keeps faith in his dealings and builds institutions meant to outlast him, knowing that orderly commerce and honest tradition alike rest on the trust that God requires of upright men.

events.fact: President Franklin Roosevelt signed the Tennessee Valley Authority Act, creating a federal effort to bring flood control, navigation, and electricity to a region long mired in poverty.
Mount St. Helens in Washington erupted catastrophically, leveling hundreds of square miles of forest and killing fifty-seven people.

block: On May 18, 1933, President Franklin Roosevelt signed the act creating the Tennessee Valley Authority, harnessing the rivers of a poor region for flood control, navigation, and electric light. On the same day in 1980, Mount St. Helens tore itself apart in a single blast, flattening ten million trees, darkening the sky for miles, and taking fifty-seven lives in moments. The works of men to tame a river and the mountain that no man could tame stand side by side as a lesson to the Steadfast citizen, who labors faithfully to better his land yet bows before the awful power of the God who made the mountains and can shake them at His word.

events.fact: The Puritan colonies of Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth, Connecticut, and New Haven formed the New England Confederation, the first union of English colonies in America, chiefly for the support of the church and the common defense.

New England's Dark Day brought an inexplicable midday darkness over the region; in Connecticut, legislator Abraham Davenport refused to adjourn, declaring that if it were the Day of Judgment he wished to be found at his duty.

block: On May 19, 1643, the Puritan colonies of Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth, Connecticut, and New Haven joined in the New England Confederation, the first union of English colonies on these shores, knit together for the defense of their people and the support of the church. On the same day in 1780, a mysterious darkness fell over New England at noon, and as many feared the end of the world had come, the Connecticut legislator Abraham Davenport answered the call to adjourn by saying that if it were indeed the Day of Judgment he chose to be found doing his duty. An Obedient citizen stands fast at the post God has given him, whether binding himself to his fellows in covenant or holding to his charge when the heavens themselves grow dark.

events.fact: President Abraham Lincoln signed the Homestead Act, granting one hundred sixty acres of public land to any citizen who would live upon it and improve it.
Charles Lindbergh took off from Roosevelt Field in New York aboard the Spirit of St. Louis, beginning the first solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic.

block: On May 20, 1862, President Abraham Lincoln signed the Homestead Act, offering a hundred and sixty acres of the public domain to any citizen willing to dwell upon the land and improve it by his own labor. On the same day in 1927, Charles Lindbergh lifted the overloaded Spirit of St. Louis off a muddy New York runway and pointed it alone across the dark Atlantic toward Paris. The homesteader breaking new ground and the airman crossing the trackless sea both answered a call that demanded faithful obedience to a hard duty, and an Obedient citizen likewise takes up the labor appointed him, trusting his way to the God who blesses honest toil and steadfast courage.

events.fact: Clara Barton founded the American Red Cross in Washington and became its first president, devoting herself to the relief of the suffering and the wounded.
Charles Lindbergh landed at Le Bourget field outside Paris, completing the first solo nonstop transatlantic flight after thirty-three and a half hours alone in the air.

block: On May 21, 1881, Clara Barton gathered a small circle in Washington to found the American Red Cross, giving her remaining strength to bind up the wounds of soldiers and the victims of disaster. On the same day in 1927, Charles Lindbergh brought the Spirit of St. Louis down at Le Bourget after thirty-three and a half hours alone over the Atlantic, holding his eyes open through the night by sheer will. The nurse who served the broken and the pilot who would not yield to exhaustion alike embody the Steadfast citizen, who perseveres in mercy and in courage, sustained by the God who renews the strength of those who will not quit.

events.fact: The SS Savannah departed from Savannah, Georgia, becoming the first steamship to cross the Atlantic Ocean; the day is now honored as National Maritime Day.
About a thousand pioneers with their wagons and livestock set out from the Missouri frontier on the Oregon Trail in the Great Emigration of 1843.

block: On May 22, 1819, the SS Savannah steamed out of her Georgia harbor to become the first steamship to cross the Atlantic, an experimental voyage so bold that the day is now kept as National Maritime Day. On the same day in 1843, roughly a thousand pioneers with their wagons and five thousand head of cattle rolled west from the Missouri frontier in the Great Emigration that opened the Oregon Trail. The mariner braving an untried ocean and the families facing two thousand miles of prairie both pressed on through hardship toward a far horizon, and a Steadfast citizen holds likewise to his course, leaning on the God who guides the wanderer and steadies the long obedience of the road.

events.fact: Benjamin Franklin described his invention of bifocal spectacles in a letter, having grown weary of switching between two pairs of glasses.
South Carolina ratified the United States Constitution at Charleston, becoming the eighth state to join the new federal union.

block: On May 23, 1785, Benjamin Franklin set down in a letter his clever remedy for failing eyes, the bifocal spectacles that let a man see both his food and the faces across the table, a small fruit of a lifetime of inventive industry. On the same day in 1788, the delegates at Charleston ratified the Constitution, making South Carolina the eighth pillar of the new federal union. Whether bending his mind to a humble invention or his judgment to the framing of a lasting government, a Steadfast citizen gives himself to careful, enduring work, knowing that the God of order honors both the patient craftsman and the faithful builder of a free people.

events.fact: Samuel Morse sent the first long-distance telegraph message from the Capitol to Baltimore, transmitting the words from Scripture, 'What hath God wrought.'
The Brooklyn Bridge opened over the East River after fourteen years of construction, then the longest suspension bridge in the world and the work of the Roebling family.

block: On May 24, 1844, Samuel Morse tapped out the first message over his telegraph line from the Capitol to Baltimore, choosing the words of Scripture, 'What hath God wrought,' to christen an invention that would bind a continent in an instant. On the same day in 1883, the Brooklyn Bridge opened after fourteen years of toil and the lifeblood of the Roebling family, joining two great cities by a span the world called a wonder. The inventor who gave God the glory for his work and the engineers who poured out their lives to finish the bridge alike call the Loyal citizen to spend his gifts faithfully in the service of others, ever mindful Whose hand makes such labors prosper.

events.fact: The Constitutional Convention reached its quorum and opened in Philadelphia, unanimously electing George Washington as its presiding officer to frame a new charter of government.
President John F. Kennedy stood before Congress and committed the nation to landing a man on the moon and returning him safely before the end of the decade.

block: On May 25, 1787, enough delegates at last gathered in Philadelphia to open the Constitutional Convention, where they rose as one to set George Washington in the chair and began the upright labor of framing a government to secure liberty. On the same day in 1961, President Kennedy summoned the nation before Congress to reach for the moon within the decade, a goal fulfilled eight years later. The grave statesmen who drafted a charter for the ages and the leader who called a people to a bold and honest endeavor both demand the integrity of an Upright citizen, who pursues great aims by straight means and keeps faith with the trust God lays upon him.

events.fact: Confederate General Edmund Kirby Smith's Trans-Mississippi forces agreed to surrender, marking the effective end of organized Confederate resistance and the close of the Civil War.
Charles Dow published the first Dow Jones Industrial Average, a new measure of American industry that began at under forty-one points with twelve companies.

block: On May 26, 1865, the surrender of General Edmund Kirby Smith's Trans-Mississippi army brought the last great Confederate force to lay down its arms, sealing the end of the Civil War and the long, costly restoration of the Union. On the same day in 1896, the financial journalist Charles Dow first published his industrial average, an honest gauge of a growing nation's commerce. An Engaged citizen takes his part both in the hard work of binding up a divided country and in the daily enterprise that sustains it, laboring for the common good as one accountable to the God who calls His people to peace and diligence.

events.fact: American forces under Colonel Winfield Scott captured Fort George on the Niagara frontier in a successful amphibious assault during the War of 1812.
The Golden Gate Bridge opened to foot traffic in San Francisco, and some two hundred thousand people crossed the great span on its first day.

block: On May 27, 1813, American troops under the young Colonel Winfield Scott stormed ashore and seized Fort George, the chief British post on the Niagara frontier, in one of the few bright American victories of that war with Britain. On the same day in 1937, the Golden Gate Bridge opened to walkers across the strait at San Francisco, the crowning achievement of years of perilous labor over a treacherous channel. The soldier pressing an assault and the builders who endured to finish their bridge both show the resolve of an Enduring citizen, who holds to the long and difficult task until it is done, strengthened by the God who sustains the patient and the brave.

events.fact: A young Lieutenant Colonel George Washington led his first military action at the Battle of Jumonville Glen in the Pennsylvania wilderness, the opening skirmish of the French and Indian War.
The steamboat Walk-in-the-Water was launched at Black Rock, New York, becoming the first steamship to navigate the Great Lakes.

block: On May 28, 1754, a twenty-two-year-old George Washington led his first command into action at Jumonville Glen, a wilderness skirmish that lit the fuse of the French and Indian War and began the schooling of the man who would father a nation. On the same day in 1818, the Walk-in-the-Water slid into the water near Buffalo, the first steamboat to ply the Great Lakes and open their waters to honest commerce. The young officer learning obedience under fire and the shipwrights opening a new frontier alike call the Obedient citizen to take up his duty faithfully where he is placed, trusting the providence of God to make his early labors serve ends he cannot yet see.

events.fact: The Massachusetts Bay Colony enacted the 'Old Deluder Satan' school law, requiring towns to provide schooling so that every child might learn to read the Scriptures, a foundation of public education in America.
Rhode Island ratified the United States Constitution by a vote of thirty-four to thirty-two, becoming the last of the original thirteen states to join the union.

block: On May 29, 1647, the Massachusetts Bay Colony passed the law men have called the 'Old Deluder Satan Act,' requiring every town of size to teach its children to read so that no one would be kept from the Scriptures by ignorance, and so laying the cornerstone of American schooling. On the same day in 1790, Rhode Island at last ratified the Constitution by the narrowest of votes, the final original state to take its place in the union and keep faith with its sister states. A Trustworthy citizen guards what is entrusted to him, whether the minds of children given the means to read God's Word for themselves or the solemn compact of a people pledged to stand together under law.

events.fact: The first national Decoration Day was observed at Arlington National Cemetery, where the graves of more than twenty thousand Civil War dead were honored with flowers; the day grew into Memorial Day.
The Lincoln Memorial was dedicated in Washington before fifty thousand people, with Abraham Lincoln's surviving son Robert Todd Lincoln present.

block: On May 30, 1868, the first national Decoration Day was kept at Arlington, where thousands gathered to strew flowers upon the graves of more than twenty thousand fallen soldiers and to remember the price of the Union, a remembrance that became our Memorial Day. On the same day in 1922, the Lincoln Memorial was dedicated before a great throng in Washington, with the martyred president's own son looking on. The honoring of the war dead and the raising of a temple to a fallen leader alike teach a Steadfast citizen to hold fast the memory of those who gave all, and to be faithful in his own generation to the God for whose justice and mercy they bled.

events.fact: President George Washington signed the first United States Copyright Act, securing to authors the fruit of their labors for the stated purpose of the 'encouragement of learning.'

The South Fork Dam failed above Johnstown, Pennsylvania, loosing a wall of water that killed more than two thousand people; the new American Red Cross under Clara Barton answered with its first great relief effort.

block: On May 31, 1790, President George Washington signed the nation's first Copyright Act, securing to authors the fruit of their minds for the express end of the encouragement of learning. On the same day in 1889, the South Fork Dam gave way above Johnstown, Pennsylvania, and a thirty-foot wall of water swept more than two thousand souls to their deaths in minutes, drawing Clara Barton and her young Red Cross to their first great work of mercy. The law that nurtured honest learning and the catastrophe that called forth selfless aid both summon a Steadfast citizen to labor faithfully in calm and to stand firm in disaster, trusting his life and his works to the sovereign God who orders all our days.
